(president borrell, president prodi, honourable members of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, i am very pleased to be here today at this first plenary session of the new european parliament. i would like to take this opportunity to congratulate all members, from across the twenty-five member states of the european union, on their election last month in the greatest supranational exercise in democracy that the world has ever known. it is good to see familiar faces and new faces alike.) mr president, i see that some members are having difficulty receiving their irish language interpretation. perhaps when irish is fully recognised in europe we will have one difficulty less. i am very pleased to be here today at the first plenary session of the new european parliament. i would like to take the opportunity to congratulate all members, from across the 25 member states of the european union, on their election last month in the greatest supranational exercise in democracy that the world has ever known. it is good to see familiar faces and new faces alike in this new parliament. i would also like, president borrell, to congratulate you on your election to the post of president of the european parliament and to wish you well. in ireland, and particularly as outgoing presidency, we are very conscious of the crucial and constructive role played by the parliament in the work of the european union. during our presidency we enjoyed an immensely cooperative and mutually supportive relationship with the european parliament, which was an essential element in the realisation of many of our presidency goals. i wish you every success in the exercise of your office over the coming years. i have come here today to report on the outcome of the june european council and on the work of the irish presidency of the council for the first six months of 2004. before i do, however, i want to outline the two key principles which underlined ireland's presidency and indeed underpin ireland's general approach to european affairs. the first and most basic principle that informed our approach was that europe must work ­ and must be seen to work ­ for its people. too often, the debate on european issues can drift into a world of jargon and theory. in doing so it runs a real risk of losing the attention and, in due course, the support of its citizens. the european union is not a matter of theory. it has and will continue to make a real difference to the lives of its citizens. without it, europe could not have recovered from the devastation of the world wars. without it, europe could not have created a vibrant single market and a strong and stable single currency. without it, we would not have had the frameworks of social and environmental protection which are the cornerstones of the european model. and, of course, without it we would not have been in a position to embrace and support the europeans who have suffered half a century of totalitarian oppression. we all need to focus on making the new enlarged european union relevant and responsive to our citizens. to do so we need to focus on that which unites us rather than that which divides us. we need to focus on the key concerns of the citizen: jobs, social and environmental protection, peace and security. they have been the ingredients of europe's success. they must remain at the centre of our attention as leaders, legislators and europeans. the second principle that has underpinned our approach to europe has been the principle of fairness. whether you are large or small - as ireland is - rules matter. the fair, even-handed and transparent application of those rules matters even more. the european union has created a zone where the concerns of all can be respected, the identities of all can be strengthened and the fundamental interests and rights of all can be protected. it is essential that the traditions of equality, fairness and cooperation that have been the keystones of the european union be reinforced in the new enlarged union. when i addressed this house in january, i set out five main areas of work for the irish presidency. we wanted a speedy and successful outcome to the work of the intergovernmental conference. we wanted a successful enlargement and we wanted to progress the ongoing enlargement negotiations. we were determined that the spring european council would help to revitalise and reinvigorate the lisbon strategy. i reported comprehensively on this issue to parliament in march 2004. in the justice and home affairs area we wanted to deliver on the commitments made in the amsterdam treaty and in the tampere programme. last, but by no means least, we sought to give renewed coherence and impetus to the european union’s external agenda. one of the main issues on our agenda, and one on which, i am delighted to say, we had a successful outcome, was the nomination of the new president of the european commission. josé manuel durão barroso played a full part in the search for the next president of the commission. it was only towards the end of the process that he allowed his name to go forward as a candidate for the position. i was therefore very pleased that the european council by consensus agreed to propose mr durão barroso as its nominee for president of the european commission. at such a crucial time in the union's development we could not have found a better candidate. he is a man who is prepared to lead and is able to take decisions. he is a committed european and has a deep understanding of the interests of all member states, large and small, old and new. i have no hesitation in recommending him to you. i am also delighted that it was possible to reach agreement on other important appointments. javier solana, who has been outstanding in his present functions, will continue in the post of secretary-general of the council, and pierre de boissieu will continue as deputy secretary-general. on the entry into force of the european constitution, following its ratification in every member state, secretary-general and high representative solana is set to become the union’s first foreign minister. a particular highlight of our presidency was, of course, the agreement we reached on a new constitution at the intergovernmental conference on 18 june. this was the culmination of more than two-and-a-half years' work that began with the laeken declaration in december 2001. the new constitution is a tribute to the commitment and political will of all of the participants in the european convention and the intergovernmental conference. today, nonetheless, i want to pay a special tribute to the work of the european parliament. throughout the process, in the european convention and the igc, parliament has shown a deep sense of commitment to the european union and to the citizens whose interests it directly represents. the convention outcome in particular - the great bulk of which was unaltered in the intergovernmental conference - reflected much that was brought to the table by the representatives of this parliament. i am conscious, too, that in the course of the intergovernmental conference the same positive, flexible and constructive attitude was struck throughout. i want to acknowledge especially the hard work that was done to find solutions to issues of particular concern to parliament, and which was essential to finding an overall agreement. a final deal would not have been possible without the assistance and commitment of parliament. i want to express my warmest thanks to you all, in particular to mr brok and mr hänsch and, of course, the former president of the european parliament, mr cox. they gave enormous help, assistance and commitment to me and mr roche, my minister for europe, who is with me today. we deeply appreciate all their help. you will all be more than familiar at this stage with the contents of the constitution. i would still nonetheless like to highlight some of the features that make it such a positive step forward for the union. we have succeeded in setting down clearly in one single document what the union is and what the union does. we have defined a set of values and objectives that we can all share and which make the european union unique across the world. we have enhanced the democratic legitimacy of the european union by extending the powers of the european parliament. we have also strengthened the role of national parliaments and opened the council of ministers to more public scrutiny. we have clarified the division of powers between the union and the member states. it is now clear how decisions are taken, and who is entitled to take them. the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality have also been strengthened. we have incorporated the charter of fundamental rights as an integral part of the constitution. in a significant advance in the area of human rights, the union's institutions and the member states when implementing union law will be bound by the charter, and the union's citizens will have the right to legal redress if they feel their rights have not been upheld. in addition, the union is to accede to the european convention on human rights, which will help to ensure consistency between the courts in strasbourg and luxembourg. we have agreed an institutional framework that fully respects the rights of all member states in all of the union's institutions. each member state will nominate a member of the commission until 2014. at that time a move will be made to a smaller commission with members from two-thirds of the member states selected on the basis of absolutely equal rotation, unless the european council decides unanimously to fix a different size. we have thus provided the basis for an effective commission into the future which, i know you agree, is of crucial importance for the union. the principle of double majority voting, enshrining the dual nature of the union as a union of states and citizens, will be implemented in a way that respects the concerns of all igc participants and enhances the efficiency of decision-making. the new team presidency arrangements bringing three member states together to implement an agreed programme will help the council to become more effective and efficient. the new permanent president of the european council, foreign minister and external action service will enhance coordination and allow the union to play a more effective role in the wider world. these are all remarkable achievements, which many would have believed impossible at the outset of the convention process. i thank all those in the convention, all those who helped us, my good colleague the president of the commission mr prodi, his colleagues who worked so hard to help us in our work, and, of course, mr giscard d'estaing, who was the president of the convention. work is now getting under way to prepare the text for signature by heads of state or government on 29 october in rome. following signature, attention will focus on ratification, which is intended to be concluded at the latest by 1 november 2006. some member states will hold referendums, others will ratify the text using parliamentary procedures. irrespective of the choices made by member states, it is incumbent on us all to explain what is in the constitution, and why it will be so beneficial for the union, the member states and especially our citizens. the questions posed at the european council in laeken in december 2001 - how to make the union more effective and efficient; how to prepare it to play a more effective role in the wider world, and how to bring the union closer to its citizens - have been well answered. our new constitution will equip us to meet, with confidence, the challenges that the union is facing as it continues to widen and deepen. the union has undergone a lengthy and exhaustive process of treaty change in recent years. it is now time for us to have the confidence to see the new constitution as the union's bedrock in the same way that the treaty of rome has served us so well over the course of more than half a century. our focus must now turn fully to formulating and implementing those policies our citizens expect of us. as our union enlarges, continuing to be able to take decisions that will serve the needs of our people will be critical. the new european constitution will enable the union to engage constructively with the future challenges and opportunities that it will face. during our six-month term as presidency, ireland was honoured and privileged to welcome 10 new member states into the european union on 1 may. we marked the occasion by a formal and symbolic ceremony - a 'day of welcomes' - in dublin. this was a truly historic moment for the european union. it was a moment of great opportunity and hope for all the people of europe. of course, the enlargement process did not end on 1 may. we are delighted to have achieved substantial progress in negotiations with bulgaria and romania. the european council noted with great satisfaction that bulgaria had provisionally closed negotiations in all outstanding chapters. in addition, romania made significant progress, provisionally closing negotiations in three chapters of the acquis. as an example of a very concrete step towards accession, work has just commenced, under the dutch presidency, on the drafting of the accession treaty. we encourage both countries to maintain and accelerate their efforts and look forward to their accession in january 2007, if they are ready. the june european council welcomed the significant progress which turkey has continued to make in the reform process, and the sustained efforts of the turkish government to meet the copenhagen political criteria. the union has reaffirmed its commitment that, if the december european council decision on the fulfilment of the political criteria is positive, accession negotiations with turkey will be opened without delay. this decision will be taken on the basis of the commission's report and recommendation. it will be taken in an objective and transparent manner. also in june the european council decided that croatia is a candidate for membership and that negotiations should begin early in 2005. our presidency had responsibility for managing the initial phase of negotiations on the future financial perspectives which will determine funding for the union from 2007 to 2013. our aim was to examine the commission's ideas in detail and to offer feedback to the commission in preparing its legislative proposals. this we did, and the june european council found the report we prepared to be a useful contribution. in june we also agreed to reach political agreement on the dossier next year. the focus of our presidency in the justice and home affairs area was on the delivery of commitments under the amsterdam treaty and in the broader tampere programme for the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice. the last six months saw very substantial progress. we adopted the asylum qualifications directive and achieved political agreement on the asylum procedures directive. the two cornerstones for a common asylum system are now in place. we moved the agreement on establishing a european border management agency forward. this is a significant measure in the effort to fight illegal immigration. we also reached political agreement on the admission of third country nationals for studies and related purposes which recognises the positive contribution that legal migration makes to the union. we worked to facilitate better access to justice across borders for citizens of the union, adopting, for example, the victims of crime directive to ensure compensation to victims of violent crime. 2004 marks the end of this five-year tampere programme. in june the european council agreed that the time had come to launch the next phase of the process and the commission will now prepare proposals for consideration in december. in the related area of terrorism, and in the aftermath of the appalling terrorist attacks in madrid, the march european council adopted the declaration on combating terrorism. in june we noted the significant progress made in implementing the measures set out in the declaration and the work of the european union counter-terrorism coordinator. the next steps are now mapped out in the revised plan of action, which was also adopted in june. in the external relations area we sought to give renewed coherence and impetus to the european union’s complex external agenda guided by the european security strategy adopted by the european council last december. i believe that our efforts in this area were very successful. we emphasised effective multilateralism, conflict prevention and the development of a european security and defence policy. we worked to strengthen and develop key partnerships, including the transatlantic relationship, on the basis of our shared interests and values. we worked hard to ensure that the millennium development goals, with their strong emphasis on poverty eradication and sustainable development and the hiv/aids pandemic, were given the high focus that they deserve. many of you in this parliament follow closely a range of external relations issues which are of particular interest to you and your constituents. you know, therefore, the progress that has been made during the past six months and what remains to be done in many challenging areas. across the range of issues - be it the transatlantic relationship, the european union's engagement with africa or the need to strengthen our relations with russia and with asia - we can report real and lasting progress. we have circulated a report on ireland's presidency of the european union to each member of parliament which sets out the key developments in the external agenda for our six-month term, as well as developments in relation to the union's internal agenda. i will be happy to respond to your queries in the debate that follows. it has been a challenging and rewarding six months for us all. at the beginning of the presidency, when i addressed this house, i said that our overall objective was to secure outcomes that would have a positive impact on the lives of europe's people. i strongly believe that, with the successful enlargement of the union, the agreement on the european constitution, the good progress made over the last six months on the lisbon agenda and justice and home affairs, as well as in our relationships with key partners, the union has made a great step forward. we must all continue to work to communicate better with our citizens so that they can become better informed and engaged in relation to developments within the union which affect their daily lives in so many positive ways. i have no doubt that the netherlands presidency will be as successful as we know it will be challenging. like parliament, i wish it well. the theme of ireland's presidency was 'europeans working together'. during the last six months, i believe that the council and the european parliament have worked together in an exemplary way. the experience has left me firmly convinced that, working together cooperatively - as member states and institutions - we can build a better europe and contribute to a fairer, more secure and more peaceful world. it is a great honour for me to report on the six months of the irish presidency, but it is not just on the six months, because in any presidency there is a lead-in of about a year. thus, for the last 18 months i have been dealing with the leaders of the groups in parliament. i wish to thank them for the time they gave to me and their visit to dublin in december 2003. they gave me very good advice. throughout the presidency both minister cowen and minister roche in particular were here many times. courtesy was shown to all my colleagues. we were determined to work closely with parliament, to give it a lot of time, listen to its views and to president of the commission. mr president, mr taoiseach, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate the new president on his recent election and i am pleased to see the elected members of parliament from all the member states finally gathered in parliament in an enlarged assembly. the new europe is being felt for the first time in this house, and that is an exciting and significant fact. our union now needs the instruments to decide and to act. this is in line with what the taoiseach has just said about the achievements of the irish presidency and, above all, the results of the european council. i congratulate the irish presidency, and bertie in particular, and his collaborators, on their diplomatic skill, political sense and great dedication to the european cause. firstly, the intergovernmental conference concluded last semester with the agreement on the european constitution. as is well known, the last part of the constitutional process is always the most difficult and the irish presidency has guided the conference with respect for everyone's views and attention to detail. it has proposed innovative solutions, without losing the balance of the whole, and has convinced all parties that this is both a strong text and a serious and realistic compromise. in other words, this constitutional treaty is the best possible agreement today. we must not underestimate the work of the taoiseach who has personally taken the trouble to overcome the obstacles in the most sensitive areas. looking back over the last five years, we must note the extraordinary developments in our union. when i first spoke in this house on 5 may 1999, the treaty of amsterdam had just entered into force. at that time, no one thought we could have a new constitution. yet today, not only its reality, but its necessity seems obvious to us, and the reason is simple: the constitution enables the union to function more efficiently in the interests of our citizens. the constitution strengthens democracy, transparency and accountability. it contains our values and principles and provides a sound legal basis for our policies. i would like to stress that it includes the charter of fundamental rights and introduces the principle of double majority for decisions taken by the council by qualified majority. no one claims that this is a perfect constitution. the commission, as you know, would have preferred stronger powers for the union in certain areas, such as economic governance in particular. in this respect, i welcome the recent judgment of the european court of justice which clarifies certain rules of the treaty and the stability and growth pact. unanimity is still required in areas such as taxation, own resources, the financial perspective and, in part, social policy and foreign policy. however, the constitution is clearly a great step forward on the road to european integration and in the near future we must all work together and focus on the ratification process. voters will be asked to express their views on the constitution in many countries through referendums. whether it is a popular referendum or parliamentary ratification, this is the moment for clarity of position. in the coming months we will therefore have to explain to the citizens what the union is and what it is not, why we need to make it work properly and what the new rules are. we must have a thorough debate on the constitution and what it means for the future of europe. we must ensure that referendums or parliamentary votes are not merely a reflection of the political situation in each member state, but that they give a conscious and thoughtful response to real issues at european level. the real issue, as i said, is europe itself, because to reject the constitution would be a huge setback for the process of integration. i am afraid that national issues will obscure the real issues of the european debate and that short-term interests will end up undermining the progress we can make with the constitution. this means that we must first of all ask the right questions in the national debates in each country. in particular, i want to respond to a criticism that has been circulating for some time, according to which the constitution would be a step backwards in social europe. i have to say, it's not. the constitution maintains the union's common policies essentially unchanged, but it creates a framework within which the institutions can act in the common interest with greater care. this applies both to measures relating to the internal market and to social policy. i would remind you, honourable members, that the constitution also goes a few steps further. full employment and social progress become the union's objectives and gender equality and the rights of minorities are recognised as values common to the member states. it also states that the union is to promote economic, social and territorial cohesion and solidarity between member states, that the union formally recognises and promotes the role of the social partners at european level and facilitates their dialogue in full respect of their autonomy, and that the union's trade policy must not impede the organisation of social services, education and health. finally, the value of services of general interest and their role in promoting social and territorial cohesion is recognised. the constitution as a whole is therefore more ambitious, more coherent and more comprehensive than the current treaties, including in the social field. these are essentially political points, not technical, and we must continue the political work to move in this direction. the level of attention to social europe is increasing among our citizens and a more political union will therefore serve to consolidate it. i therefore call on all members to ensure that the citizens know what the real issues are when we have to ratify the constitution. voting yes to the constitution also means voting for this different framework of social europe. the constitution is certainly a historic achievement, but it is not the only decision taken by the last european council. among other things, i would like to mention the recognition of croatia as a candidate country. this decision confirms the union's will to offer the troubled countries of this region of our continent a prospect of accession. now that the council is satisfied that croatia meets the copenhagen criteria, negotiations can start as early as the beginning of 2005. the government of macedonia has also submitted its application for membership and is making a determined effort to have it accepted. in the area of justice and home affairs, the action plan on combating terrorism has seen much progress, but also some uncertainties. progress is being made on the tampere programme, but it must now enter a new phase of implementation. the council also called on the member states to complete the implementation of the measures linked to the lisbon strategy. this is a complicated area where the steps and progress made are not enough and, above all, do not correspond to the expectations we had in lisbon when we approved this chapter. finally, i congratulate the irish presidency on reaching agreement on the name of josé manuel durão barroso, which was unanimously approved by the council, an agreement which i regard as a masterpiece of democracy and politics. i also welcome the decision to appoint javier solana as the union's foreign minister once the constitution has entered into force. i would like to extend my warmest congratulations to josé manuel durão barroso and javier solana and my sincere thanks to bertie ahern and her colleagues.

president of the council. president, members of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen,i am very pleased to present the priorities of the dutch presidency to you, the directly elected representatives of the european citizens. as members of the european parliament, you hold one of the most beautiful and important offices in the european union. it is not for nothing that parliament is the first institution mentioned in the treaty. you are the guardian of the quality of our community, which is above all a community of values. you have been given a fine commission by the citizens great sense of responsibility. for europe, for the substantive dossiers we want to take forward, but above all with regard to the people of europe, for whom we are all doing this. i would like to one work shows europe as a maze. another like a tower under construction. a third like a drowning man trying to climb out of the water. there are many different ways of looking at europe. how does the europeans turned out to vote. there is a general lack of confidence and doubt among certain groups of citizens in the european integration process. the european project is being closely monitored, both outside and inside the european parliament. the dutch presidency is fully aware of this. but critical voices are part of a democracy. they can make a democracy stronger. there is no reason to be pessimistic. on the contrary: it is now time to show the european citizens that europe is theirs. a work in progress. not perfectly. it's subject to improvement. but it is valuable and - as history has taught us - it is very necessary to tackle problems that no country can solve alone. that is what makes the european union worth contributing actively to. the dutch presidency wants to send that message with a vigour. with ambition in the heart and realism in the head. cooperation with you is of the utmost importance. whether you are one of those who see europe as a maze. or like a tower under construction. you all represent the views of the european citizens. it's about them. we want to work with you to take concrete steps that citizens will recognise and accept. i realize that the coming period is a time for you when innovations must be made concrete. the european parliament has been enlarged to 732 members. 162 representatives from the 10 new member states have joined parliament and must find their way. political families change their composition and add new members. it is gratifying to see you taking up your duties with determination and pursuing the legislative activities of this parliament with energy. there is more innovation to come. the new constitution considerably increases the european parliament's influence on decision-making and the conduct of affairs in the union. the national parliaments will also have an important role to play in answering the question of whether european legislation is necessary in specific cases. the union will thus become more democratic. the citizens' voice will be heard louder and stronger under the new constitution. the new constitution also improves the situation of those who are critical of european integration. the dutch presidency welcomes the extension of the european parliament's powers. this is one of the main strengths of the new treaty and therefore also an important argument in the national debates on approval. the adoption of this directive will be accompanied by vigorous discussions in a number of countries. i hope that the facts will not be weighed against the images. the new constitution will undoubtedly bring the union closer to its citizens. is that not what we all want most? it is particularly in this time of renewal that it is important to stay the course and ensure that we continue to make progress for the benefit of the european citizen. without proper cooperation between the council, parliament and the commission, this cannot be achieved. the dutch presidency would like to work constructively with you. and we hope with all our hearts that you will also cooperate constructively with us. the presidency, like many in this chamber, regrets that the lingering problem of the statute for members has not yet been resolved. the previous president worked very hard on this with your support, but no result has yet been achieved. if there is any prospect of a solution, the dutch presidency will certainly cooperate in that regard. it is not possible to cover all the substantive issues on the agenda within the scope of this presentation. i shall therefore confine myself to those issues which require our joint attention in particular. without wanting to prejudge future presidencies, it is clear that we must dare to look beyond 1 january 2005. we are well aware that objectives must be achieved over a series of years. the dutch presidency is a link in a chain. that is why we are trying to create the best possible conditions for the work of the next presidencies. the dutch presidency will always seek to take account of the longer-term interests. if we want to give something of ourselves to the union, it is a future orientation. internally, by working towards consolidating the enlarged union, sustainable economic growth, security and a solid financial base for the years ahead. externally, by looking ahead together with our partners elsewhere in the world and acting more effectively as a union on the world stage. firstly, the consolidation of the union. the ten countries which joined on 1 may this year must be able to feel at home in the union as soon as possible. this is a particular responsibility of the presidency. we will do our utmost to ensure that the new member states can participate fully in all the union's working processes as soon as possible. at the same time, we want to lay a solid foundation for future enlargements. the accession negotiations with bulgaria have recently been completed. those with romania are at an advanced stage. the accession negotiations with croatia will start next year. and in december the european council will consider whether turkey meets the political criteria of copenhagen in the field of human rights and democracy. if so, accession negotiations will also be opened with that country. the decision-making process must be fair, according to the rules of the game to which we previously committed ourselves with full conviction in 2002. that means: the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. we must not be guided by fear, for example of islam. the european community of values does not want to impose restrictions on a particular religion. our resistance should not be directed against religions but against individuals and groups who abuse their religion to enforce their will by violence. (applause from the left) islam is not the problem. muslims, christians and people of other faiths can live together very well. the problem is not religion, but the misuse of religion to sow hatred and intolerance and to oppress women. this does not change the fact that the decision on turkey is very much concerning and disturbing to many. the presidency wishes to make it possible to reach a well-founded decision, one which is supported by all and which will remain firmly established in the future. the second theme on the agenda is also about looking to the future: sustainable economic growth. the european economy is gradually recovering from a period of stagnation. but recovery is slow and difficult, because of the underlying weaknesses in our economic structure. the european economy is stiff-necked and uses its head too little. that's why our competitors are outsmarting us. if we look at developments objectively, we see that europe is losing ground even in times of economic recovery. we should not keep our eyes on our own jobs, our own social safety net, our own pension. but on the job, the social safety net and our children's pensions. how strong will europe be in a few decades? can our children and grandchildren build a good life in europe? can we then continue to put our values of solidarity and social justice into practice? please note: these are not things to be taken for granted. look at the rapid development of countries like china and india. is europe strong and flexible enough to cope with this competition? it is against this background that we must give the highest priority to the implementation of the lisbon strategy. the preparations for the mid-term evaluation of these will be made during the dutch presidency. a working group led by wim kok is currently preparing a report on what we have achieved so far and what remains to be done. this report will be presented to the european council on 5 november. europe is missing out on considerable opportunities. we are not getting what is in our internal market. the services market in particular is still subject to a variety of national barriers. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. we are not thereby exploiting the power of the single market. if we know that 1.8 per cent of european gdp and 2.5 million jobs are currently due to the functioning of the internal market, then we have every reason to strengthen and extend the internal market towards the services sector. the services directive proposed by the european commission is an important step in the right direction. it goes without saying that the rapid adoption of this legislation can be a major support for the european economy. the functioning of the internal market can also be improved by less and better regulation. we need to make the rules work for us instead of us working for the rules. the irish, dutch, luxembourg and united kingdom presidencies have jointly given priority to this. much of the ambition of the lisbon agenda will have to be achieved within the member states. labour markets need to become more flexible and social security systems more active. pension systems need to be built on a stronger foundation so that future generations can build on it. in the global economy of today and tomorrow, europe must not only have its flexibility, but also its knowledge. europe's capacity for innovation is not strong enough. let me give you one example. some 400 000 european scientists are currently working in the united states. they make up 40 percent of the american scientific community. a massive exodus of people that we ourselves so desperately need. that is why we must continue vigorously to improve the knowledge environment in europe. one of the concrete measures is the creation of a european research council, aimed at making risk capital available for research. (applause) our ambitions are not just about economic growth, but also about sustainability. the dutch presidency will work to strengthen the environmental dimension of the lisbon process, with particular attention to sustainable mobility, clean technology and international climate policy. (applause from the left) the union is more than an economic project. it is also still a project of freedom, solidarity and mutual respect, 60 years after d-day. of the intangible matters that citizens are particularly concerned about, security is the most important. the increase in security has always been a driving force behind european cooperation. once upon a time, there was a shaky peace on a war-torn continent. now, new threats are forcing us to act. terrorism and organised crime. threats that we can only master together. it is essential that we continue to look forward together. with the tampere programme coming to an end, new steps are needed to further expand the european area of freedom, security and justice. the dutch presidency is seeking to ensure that the european council of 5 november sets out as concrete a perspective as possible. in a free europe with open internal borders, it is inevitable that we will align our criminal justice systems and that our cooperation will be watertight. the union must not offer legal and geographical hills of refuge to criminals who abuse the freedom that europe offers them. and sometimes we'll have to leap over our own shadow. countries are sometimes very attached to their national tradition in the area of policing and justice. but without further coordination in these areas, we remain at risk of criminals breaking the dance and endangering our security. the european counter-terrorism coordinator gijs de vries last month outlined how europe can more effectively stop terrorism. the dutch presidency intends to work diligently on the elaboration and implementation of the proposed action points. the dutch presidency will also prioritise a new european drugs strategy for 2005-2012. this will focus on the joint approach to large-scale drug trafficking, but also on better prevention and health care. there can be tension between freedom and security. neither can ever be absolute. it's all about finding the right balance. we must also find that balance in the area of asylum and migration; the european council will be discussing the tampere follow-up to the european council of 5 november. we do not want to create a fortress europe. but we also see how hectic the dynamics are of incoming and transit asylum seekers and illegal immigrants. smugglers make unscrupulous use of it. we also know from experience how much is involved in providing newcomers with full opportunities in our society. so controlling migration flows is necessary, and we can only do that together. in a union with open internal borders, we cannot avoid a european policy on asylum, migration and return. as foreseen in the tampere programme, we are entering a phase of further harmonisation. our aim is to establish a common asylum system and to provide better protection for refugees in their regions of origin. we must fight illegal immigration together, on the basis of solidarity between member states. we cannot do that without effective surveillance of our external borders. the external border control agency is crucial to this. we must now ensure that this can be operational by 2005. europe is a place for all who are entitled to it. by "place", i mean much more than a shelter. it's about a place in our society. we want to pay more attention to the integration of newcomers. member states have their own traditions in this area. there must be room for that. but i think we can learn more from each other's experiences. a credible asylum and migration policy also requires the return of those who have no right to stay here. the dutch presidency has the task of making progress on the return policy before the end of the year. this includes joint return procedures and operations and the establishment of return and readmission agreements. the last important item on our internal agenda that i would like to mention is the financial basis for the coming years. in 2005, the negotiations on the next multiannual budgetary framework of the union will be finalised: the financial perspective. this is a sensitive subject. there are many different views on this. the dutch presidency sees it as its responsibility to structure these extremely complex negotiations as well as possible in advance, by agreeing guidelines and principles for the negotiations this year. it'll make it easier to get the job done. the european parliament will of course be closely involved in the preparation of the adoption of the new financial perspective. a union that looks to the future also looks to the world around it. our future is closely linked to that of our neighbours and our partners elsewhere in the world. we are a union of 25 developed countries. a community built on the values of freedom, solidarity and respect for one another. and the largest economic bloc in the world. the world rightly looks at us with a look of expectation. are we living up to those expectations? europe could be more effective. we could achieve more if we all came together and spoke with one voice. the major global issues of our time are the fight against terrorism, the promotion of human rights and democracy, economic development and the fight against poverty. in these areas europe must make a single, powerful voice. the european security strategy provides an excellent basis for this, not least because of the broad vision it contains. it is more than the development of own crisis management capacities. the dutch presidency will work in all possible ways to implement the security strategy. the united nations is the heart of multilateral cooperation and must remain so. the netherlands, as president of the european council, will play an active role in the debate on the reform of the united nations. the multilateral trading system will also need to be given a further boost. after the failure of cancun, we have a chance this year to make real progress in the wto. everyone has a stake in this. the latest as president of the european council. the european union is faced with a paradox in our time, in 2004. on the one hand, we see the dream of the founders of the european union come true. the european countries have dared to join their destinies. and have brought about reconciliation, stability and prosperity. well, in hindsight, that's a great accomplishment. on the other hand, it is becoming increasingly clear that this cooperation and sense of belonging is no longer a natural part of the experience of many people. it seems like we're having a harder time identifying the common denominator. it's like we don't see clearly what connects us most deeply. that's something to think about. the union is intensively working on its enlargement. the builder must be careful to keep the people. in concrete terms, we will be holding a number of conferences and launching initiatives to stimulate the debate on europe with the citizens of europe. we hope that this will help to raise awareness among european citizens of what it means to be european. the special value of europe lies in the fact that we are a community in which freedom, solidarity and mutual respect are balanced. the agenda i have presented to you is based on these three fundamental values. freedom of speech: that means working on security and deepening cooperation with our partners in the world. solidarity with the other countries that means working for economic growth and social cohesion, for future and current generations. respect . this means working towards understanding and mutual commitment in the enlarging union with all its differences. ladies and gentlemen, the european union is not perfect. but that's no reason to write her off or to be careless with her. it's not criticism we should fear, we are leaving behind a completely new institutional structure. it has been a great privilege to lead this college and its personalities form an extraordinary team of value, of which all european citizens can be proud. the greatest achievement of these five years was the final breaking down of the wall that had divided the continent for half a century. on 1 may, a political masterpiece was achieved and the union was able to express the strength of its model and the values on which it is based more clearly than ever before: the european union is a great example of this. i am convinced the european model can help these peoples so close to us to overcome the old divisions and the old tragedies. with the new neighbourhood policy we have found an original and realistic formula for proposing a new model of ever closer relations with our new neighbours, creating a ring of friendly countries throughout the region from morocco to russia. the launching of the creation of a new large political, economic and human region was one of the major strategic objectives of this commission. today, this objective is a political reality. during these five years, the commission has also promoted the economic and social renewal of the union and has worked to ensure macroeconomic stability. the most important action was undoubtedly the introduction of the euro. the single currency has already fulfilled its promise of stability and in these difficult years for the world economy, economies have shown themselves to be well able to withstand external shocks. there has been no exchange rate shock, no public finance crisis, not even in the difficult times of the last few months, and inflation has remained low. think what would have happened if we had not had the single currency. finally, we must remember that the mandate of this commission saw the birth of the text of the first constitution for europe, which i have already spoken of at length this morning. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, if the euro, enlargement and the constitution are the most visible achievements, we must not forget the other achievements of this commission. i should like to mention, without listing them all, the extraordinary work done on state aid and the management of the stability and growth pact. in this work the commission has remained true to its role as guardian of the treaties and has ensured absolute equality of treatment for all the parties concerned, large and small countries. we can discuss the rules we have set ourselves, we can see how to change them, how to make them more appropriate to the new economic reality, but it is the commission's duty to apply the existing rules impartially, pursuing only the common interest. i cannot help recalling the continuing work of building the internal market, in which we have often had to overcome the resistance and lack of cohesion of the member states. but thanks to this work, european consumers today spend less on flying, connecting to the internet and making payments from one country to another in the union than they did five years ago. it should also be added that there is no genuine growth in the european project unless it involves all the regions of the union. this action has, over the years, considerably reduced the differences in income and development prospects between the regions of our territory. this is an exceptional fact because usually in large economic aggregates if you do not provide strong policy, the richer areas get richer and the poorer areas get poorer. of course, more must be done in this direction in the future, especially to meet the demand for solidarity from the new member states. moreover, while the euro provides financial stability, our future growth depends on the renewal of our economic system as envisaged by the lisbon agenda. as you know, this is still a sore point because the results are not up to expectations, but i assure you that the project would have been completely stranded without our constant pressure on the member states. we are almost at the end of the strategy projected for the whole decade and much remains to be done. i thank prime minister balkenende for his commitment to this path, which is still the one that has produced less favourable results than we hoped. the commission has, however, laid a solid foundation for the final success of the operation. as the lisbon agenda is based both on the renewal of the economy and on the creation of a truly competitive knowledge society, we have substantially increased, for what we could afford, funding for research, education and training in europe. together with the projects for the creation of networks of excellence, we leave to the next commission our proposal to double the community research budget over the period 2007-2013, thus setting an example of a strong choice for all member states. as far as education is concerned, one of the highlights of the mandate was the day when the millionth university student went abroad to study under the erasmus programme. one million is an extraordinary figure and by the end of the decade we will triple that. the removal of these barriers will help to create the knowledge society, but it will also help to raise a generation of genuine european citizens, since mobility and european citizenship are closely linked and it is by focusing on young people and students that we lay the foundations for the union of tomorrow. i am therefore very pleased that the dutch presidency is making mobility and young people one of its priorities. the same concept applies to the external borders. it is essential to make full use of the external dimension of european policies relating to education, training and youth. for this reason, this commission has launched university cooperation and exchange programmes with the mediterranean, the balkans and central asia. the latest addition to this family is erasmus mundus, a crucial programme which will bring thousands of students from all over the world to our universities and will serve to restore europe's leading role in research and higher education. this is precisely the objective that balkenende outlined earlier, without which europe will not be able to achieve the lisbon objectives. after having recalled some of the achievements of this mandate, honourable members, let us follows the political programme adopted last february. the strategy is simple: we have first defined the political priorities for the period after 2007 and then put on the table the framework of the minimum financial resources needed to achieve these objectives. we have therefore focused on the content and the political objectives and not just on the financial aspects. i am satisfied with the great work done because we are up to the new tasks which the european council has given to the commission. in 2007 the union will have over 100 million new citizens, and yet our proposal leaves the current ceiling of own resources unchanged, because, thanks to strict, indeed very strict, budgetary discipline and careful planning, we can even bring the union's member states to 27 by spending on average only 1.14% of gross national income. the reality is that europe can really make a difference, but if the financial resources are lacking, european added value will be zero. we have prepared our proposals with the aim of maximising the efficiency of community spending by demonstrating, chapter by chapter, that one euro spent at european level is worth more than one euro spent at national level. otherwise, we didn't make any offers. the union's priorities, as the european council has repeatedly stated, are competitiveness, european citizenship and europe's role in the world. we have taken these decisions very seriously and we have the task of finding the appropriate resources in the community budget for their implementation because they are tasks which have been entrusted to us by the european council. all the institutions - the commission, the council and parliament - have a common duty to honour their commitments and to respond to the expectations of the citizens. if the european union fails to deliver on its promises, it is bound to lose the confidence of its citizens. after 1 may 2004, we continued our efforts to achieve european unification. the negotiations with bulgaria are technically over. as regards romania, i intend to do everything in my power to bring the negotiations forward as quickly as possible, thus respecting the commitments which - i must remind you all - provide for the conclusion of the negotiations in 2004, provided the country is ready. at the beginning of october the commission will adopt the report and opinion on the opening of accession negotiations with turkey, which will form the basis for the council decision next december. i accepted without hesitation the mandate given to me by the european council in december 2002 to present this report on turkey's compliance with the copenhagen political criteria and to express an opinion on it. it is too early to reveal the contents of this report, but i can only say that we are gathering analysis, facts and testimonies in a 360-degree manner. i can assure you that we are doing a job which is absolutely thorough and objective. this total impartiality is due to our mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. the european parliament must play a new role in this legislature. it is also set out in the draft constitutional treaty. it is generally said that this treaty will give parliament more rights. the european parliament, on a closer look, will only gain its role if it can rely on an absolute majority of its members in its work. this is particularly true of legislative work. only if parliament acts by an absolute majority does it play its part in the triangle of power between the commission and the council. this is the constitutional reality of this house. and from this we must draw political conclusions. in the past parliament has been torn between the council and the commission all too often because there were no firm majorities and because both the council and the commission could play parliament against each other. we are therefore convinced that we must make efforts to put parliament in a position and to make it accountable. that requires political cooperation in this house. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval, and the council will then be able to take a decision on the matter. because only then is there a numerical chance of a majority in this house. and that is why the unusual picture is that parties which in their domestic, domestic national reality are usually the natural antipodes - socialists on the one hand and christian democrats and conservatives on the other - are here attempting to cooperate on a specific occasion, which in many cases is met with distrust at home. but, ladies and gentlemen, we have a different political clock. i think we should not simply subject our own rules of decision-making to national consideration. we should have enough self-awareness to make it clear that we make political decisions differently from the national domestic reality of the nation state. that is why we are calling for the establishment of a firm majority, because only then can parliament play a role in the triangle of power between the commission and the council.

commission. mr president, for many years the international civil aviation organisation has been looking at market-based options designed to limit aviation emissions and introduce the aircraft and operating practices that are best environmentally. the icao has been looking at three options: taxes on fuel or emissions, emission charges and emissions trading. unfortunately, under pressure from the united states, the council has decided to propose a resolution which recommends that the icao only pursue emissions trading and, therefore, disregard the other options. this is clearly contrary to our objectives. the commission shares the view that the european union must make the most appropriate use of all economic instruments for achieving sustainability in the aviation sector, as it does in other sectors. this means pressing to keep all options – taxation, emissions charging and emissions trading – open. this view was unanimously supported by all member states in the council, in coreper, when it was discussed in july. it is important that we keep all options open, not favouring any particular option at this stage, so that europe can decide on the best way forward, after further analysis, on the basis of realistic policy alternatives. since there is no certainty at present that any one measure will suffice, disregarding any option that might help limit the impact of aviation on climate change at this stage is not desirable. therefore, even though this will be difficult, the commission will work during the assembly to try to achieve a resolution that keeps options open. commission. it gives me pleasure to reply to mr harbour. let me deal first with the question of safety. in markets where the repair market has been liberalised, as in the united kingdom, spain, italy or the netherlands, there have been no incidences of casualties attributable to the fact that third party providers have supplied some spare parts. the safety record in liberalised markets is as good – or, if you like, as bad – but no different from the safety record in markets where there is protection of the design. secondly, believe it or not, there are 90 directives, concerned with the safety of pedestrians, which apply to all cars and parts of cars, and therefore also to parts supplied by third party suppliers. the third point is that there is a so-called 'extended impact assessment' attached to the proposal, which deals with safety – it runs to 50 pages. i can assure members of this house, particularly mr harbour, that it is a very thorough impact assessment. he and other members of parliament that express an interest will receive it, together with the proposal. the extended impact assessment deals with the issue very thoroughly, but in order to still fears and apprehensions which exist, not only here but also at the commission, i have said that, now that the proposal has been adopted, i shall see to it that a further study is carried out into the safety aspects, so that we all can rest assured that the matter is being looked at. the extended impact assessment is a very thorough job and i have held extensive consultations with stakeholders, particularly with the car industry itself. members of this house will be able to read the extended impact assessment and form their own opinions. i look forward to a discussion on this proposal in parliament, even though i personally will not take part, but will be replaced by my successor, charlie mccreevy from ireland.
commission. mr president, firstly, who will control or supervise the car market and the spare parts produced by third parties? as i said earlier, there are 90 directives concerned with the safety of automobiles and these directives are policed, if you like, by the member states. the same will therefore apply to spare parts produced by a third party. those motor vehicles and those parts will also be supervised or policed by member states. so we can rest assured on that score. secondly, and this is something i put in the directive only last night, we realise that consumers need to be adequately informed. therefore, if the spare parts are not produced by the original car manufacturer but by third parties, the buyer must be informed accordingly. so to that extent the consumer will be advised that what he is buying comes from a different factory, which will enable him to say that he does not want that spare part, he wants the original, even though it may be somewhat more expensive.
the commission has already done so. i would like to make a preliminary remark: i do not think it is a good thing that this commission has yet to decide on this important matter. i think it would have been more sensible to leave this to the next commission, perhaps with a slightly different focus. in the explanatory statement for your decision you mentioned that a new market would open up there, that it could also create jobs. in another context you spoke of impact assessment. my question is: is there an impact assessment of this job creation, or is it not that jobs are being eliminated within existing industrial jobs because these things are now being forcibly liberalized for ideological reasons, and that we are moving jobs out of the european union to non-european countries through this directive.
commission. mr president, on the first question of whether this commission should have left the issue for the next commission, i wish to say that this whole issue goes back to 1998, when a directive was adopted on the protection of designs. at that time no agreement could be reached on the issue of spare parts for cars and the matter was put on hold. however, it was agreed that any change in legislation should go in the direction of liberalisation. that is what we have done today. secondly, in 2002 my colleague, mr monti, convinced the commission and others of the need to liberalise the distribution of cars, which is called block exemption. this was done, and this proposal is the natural concomitant of his proposal, which was adopted in 2002. therefore, it was of the essence that this commission should deal with this issue because, as i have said, it goes with his proposal. i therefore insisted that this commission should deal with it. moreover, i think the member who has just spoken would agree that it would not do for this commission - even though it is within six weeks of the end of its term of office - to pass on difficult decisions to the next commission. we are paid to take decisions - even though they may be difficult - and we should do that. the second point refers to employment. at the moment car manufacturers obtain spare parts beyond and outside the european union. they buy bonnets, headlamps and rear windows in countries like turkey, brazil and korea. in other words, at the moment car manufacturers have exported jobs to those countries. if we open the market for repairs and the secondary market for spare parts, it is more than likely that the jobs created by small and medium-sized enterprises - which, we all agree, are very important for industry in general and in particular for german industry - will more than compensate for the loss of jobs as car manufacturers have been outsourcing their components - their spare parts - to suppliers beyond the confines of the european union. although it is difficult to point to hard facts, i am confident that the net result will be positive for employment, since i expect these small- and medium-sized enterprises to become very successful in the secondary market for spare parts.

question no 24 by linda mcavan (h-0231/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: statistics on unexplained sudden deaths among young peopleat the request of more than 100 members of the european parliament from all 15 member states, the world health organisation recently agreed to consider possible recommendations for improving the accuracy of national statistics on unexplained sudden deaths among young people. experts across europe lament that these deaths are recorded and classified with causes that are sometimes vague or incorrect, making it difficult to get an accurate picture of the true extent of the problem. can the commission indicate what possibilities exist for eurostat to contribute to the work of the world health organisation, in particular with regard to the training of forensic and pathological experts in the context of the statistical recording of unexplained sudden deaths?
the commission the world health organization is responsible for determining the exact classification of the items to be respected when certifying death and informing statistical authorities of the causes of death, with which we collaborate - as i mentioned in my initial reply - very closely. eurostat - the statistical agency under my responsibility as commissioner - has the greatest interest in having the most accurate information on causes of death, but what eurostat cannot do is change the current headings. the study i referred to earlier says that the headings can be improved because some of them are indeed confusing. but it is not the responsibility of eurostat, it is the responsibility of the world health organization. what eurostat does have a responsibility for - and is doing - is to facilitate the training of those who have to certify, and to that end there is a training package prepared by eurostat which basically has three elements: a basic certificate of certification at european union level, a website which serves as an on-line training tool for those who have to certify, and information on paper which is also accessible via the internet in the form of a brochure in pdf format which specifies and details for those who have to certify what the requirements are and how to collect the most accurate information possible, so that the users of that information - for the purposes you indicated and which we all share - can use it in the most effective way. so we're working on it, we're continuing that training effort, in collaboration with the world health organization. what we cannot do is take on the responsibility of changing those headings which may be causing some confusion.

commission of course, there are many levels. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am thinking in particular of a number of technical measures concerning the composition of materials, protection against certain risks and specific characteristics which are sometimes imposed, particularly in the united states or in a number of important developing countries such as brazil, south africa, egypt and india. in reality, these are trade barriers which, under the pretext of protecting a particular local characteristic, have the effect of effectively prohibiting imports and protecting local producers. the whole 'non-tariff barriers' part, of which i have just given a few examples, is part of the multilateral negotiations as we are conducting them in the doha round, and what is true for textiles also applies to other sectors such as the automobile or electronics. so this area of non-tariff barriers is also part of the negotiations we are conducting at the world trade organization.

competence to pursue family policy as such. however, given that the issue of family cuts across many different policy areas in which the commission is active, it has already contributed to an commission. reconciling work and family life is one of the main concerns of social policy. most of our legislative measures or our policies attempt to achieve this. as an example, we are shortly to have a revision of the working time directive, the provisions of which are designed to ensure reconciliation between family life and work. flexible working hours is another instance of such a policy. we are working hard on this and i hope that we will have a more detailed policy in the coming months.
question no 33 by mr papadimoulis (h-0229/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: problems in the transposition of directive 1999/70/ecarticle 11 of presidential decree 164/19.07.04 which transposed directive 1999/70/ec into greek law oj l 175, 10.7.1999, p. 43. the court of justice has held that the principle of equal treatment for men and women in the labour market is not a fundamental principle of community law. you must have worked for 24 months, have had your employment contract renewed at least once and have an 'active contract' on the deadline (19 july 2004 date of publication) or three months before that. this scheme is contrary to the provisions of directive 1999/70/ec, since it applies only to workers who reach the age of majority in mid-2004. the extension of the transposition period is therefore not only detrimental to the interests of the workers but also to the transposition of the directive into greek law, which is delayed by two years. in a letter to the greek government of 13 february 2004, the commission expressed concerns about the measures taken by the greek government in relation to a 'possible abuse due to the use of fixed-term employment contracts in the period between the expiry of the deadline for transposition into national law and the entry into force of presidential decree (81/2003) '. can the commission therefore state what measures it intends to take to abolish this type of 'active employment contract', which is contrary to directive 1999/70/ec?
the commission. of course, the question is more internal to greece and concerns the various governments and agencies, but because mr papadimoulis is referring specifically to a provision on the subject of the active contract - because that is the meaning of the previous sentence - i would like to say that firstly, this specific provision of the presidential decree - and i am talking for now, i am not referring to what happened in 2002 - does not violate the directive, since there is no obligation to convert contracts into contracts of indefinite duration. the conditions for conversion laid down in the presidential decree are the responsibility of the greek government and any dispute arising from the application of these conditions may be settled before the greek courts. in so far as the condition of having a contract in force for the persons you mentioned, who were not appointed during the period in which the directive had not been transposed into greek law, concerns the mechanism for converting contracts into contracts of indefinite duration, i would like to ask the commissioner whether he has not already taken the necessary steps to ensure that the conditions for the appointment of such persons are met. the commission is therefore not competent to take measures to abolish that condition, since such an obligation to convert contracts does not arise from the directive. as mr papadimoulis has rightly pointed out, the commission has in the past raised questions about the measures taken by the greek government to prevent abuses arising from the use of fixed-term contracts during the delay in transposing the directive into national law. the question to the commission concerned the previous presidential decree which, on the one hand, delayed the transposition of the directive and, on the other hand, transposed it poorly. if this situation had not been remedied by the new presidential decree, the commission could theoretically have initiated the procedures provided for in articles 226 and 228 to declare the member state in breach of its obligations under the treaty and to compel it to comply. in addition, because mr papadimoulis referred to the rights of citizens, the commission could indeed turn against the member state in the event of damage caused by the late and faulty transposition of a directive. there is a case law on this. in this way citizens are protected from the damage they may suffer from the inadvertent and unlawful delay in the transposition of a directive by a member state. in such a case, jurisdiction lies with the national courts and the award of damages is subject, first, to the existence of unlawful conduct by the member state - for example, late or negligent transposition of a directive into national law - and, second, to the existence of a causal link between the member state's conduct and the damage suffered. as regards the present case, since the new presidential decree does not appear to be contrary to the directive and, subject to the completion of the commission's examination procedure, there are no measures that could be taken against greece.

council. mr president, we had an interesting meeting in scheveningen. the discussion was based on three papers. first, a commission communication on the stability and growth pact; second, a court ruling on the excessive deficit procedure with reference to germany and france; and third, a statement by the european council on the stability and growth pact. ministers agreed that the commission communication offered a good basis for discussion. the discussion was held in two parts. first, we had a long discussion in the euro group with the 12. next, we discussed these conclusions in the group of 25, because the other 13 hope to become members of emu as soon as possible. the first conclusion we came to – contrary to some press interpretations – is that ministers are not seeking to water down the pact, but rather want it to be strengthened, clarified and better implemented. of course, the discussions could not be concluded in a single day, so we gave our collaborators some political guidance to enable them to work on the question in the future, together with the commission. the first thing we noticed is that, contrary to what is sometimes thought, the stability pact has proven its usefulness in anchoring budget deficits. if you compare, for example, the budget deficits in the member states during the current slowdown with earlier slowdowns, or with what is happening elsewhere in the world, it can be seen that the pact has contributed to lower deficit levels than we would otherwise have seen. if you also look at interest rates and inflation, we can be pleased with the effects of the combined budgetary and monetary policy. the second point we agreed upon is that we will not change anything as far as the 3% or 60% criteria are concerned – these are in the treaty, are of paramount importance and should not be changed. we also agreed that a rule-based system remains the best guarantee for ensuring that commitments are enforced for all member states in an equal way. we agreed that the treaty should not be changed at all and that changes to regulations should be kept to a minimum, if indeed they are needed at all, but we are not sure of that yet. in strengthening and clarifying the stability and growth pact, due consideration should be given to strengthening its economic rationale and its implementation. to ensure the credibility of the framework, rules should be kept both transparent and simple. we think the following elements should be analysed. firstly, the preventive arm of the pact should be strengthened. a more symmetrical approach to fiscal policy is needed through budgetary discipline during good times so as gradually to achieve budgetary surpluses when the upswing comes. secondly, we shall use peer pressure and peer support at an early stage of budgetary deviations, rather than waiting until a country breaches the 3% rule. thirdly, we need transparent budgetary figures and growth assumptions in order to identify and correct budgetary deviations in a timely manner. the second issue we discussed was debt and debt sustainability. the focus on these elements should be enhanced. firstly, more attention should be paid to the fact that a debt ratio should be sufficiently diminishing if it is above its reference value, approaching the reference value at a satisfactory pace. secondly, in assessing whether a member state has reached sustainable public finances, the costs of ageing should be taken into account. thirdly, we agreed to look further into the issue of debt sustainability. one particular concern centred on the possible statistical implications of pension reforms. thus concerns a few countries, but is something we should investigate further. a third important element is that when a country is subject to an excessive deficit procedure and we have to assess whether it is complying with the recommendations, we should make a clear distinction between measures taken, on the one hand, and economic forecasting errors. until now we issued recommendations on the efforts required and hoped for a result, but that result was in the same spirit as the written forecast. thus in future, when assessing whether or not a country has met the recommendations, we should make a distinction between policy mistakes and forecasting mistakes. finally, within the framework of the stability and growth pact, budgetary policies need to set the right priorities for structural reforms, innovation and competitiveness in support of the lisbon agenda to promote economic growth and create jobs. we asked the economic and financial committee and the commission to work these principles out further so we can have another discussion at ministerial level. we also agreed that it would be best to hold this discussion in parallel with discussions on france and germany and the excessive deficit procedure applied to them.
