the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr president-in-office of the council, i thank you first of all for inviting me to discuss the stability and growth pact. as you know, the european commission adopted on 3 september a communication on strengthening economic governance and clarifying the implementation and application of the stability and growth pact. i think it is very important to discuss not only in the council, as we did last weekend - and we will do in the coming weeks and months - but also in this parliament and in the national parliaments the economic governance framework and, in particular, the status and future prospects of the stability and growth pact. as the president-in-office of the council, mr zalm, said, we had a first debate on this subject last weekend in the hague, both in the eurogroup of 12 and around the table of the extended eurogroup of 25. the council has agreed that the commission's communication is a good basis for discussion and we now hope that in the coming weeks and months the work we are going to undertake at a more technical level between the representatives of the member states in the economic and financial committee and the commission will enable us to reach the november ecofin with a degree of agreement far more full of substance than we have been able to debate and reach on many points around the principles or the more general ideas among those contained in the commission's communication. as mr zalm has also said, the draft constitutional treaty adopted in june ratifies what is already included in the treaty and which we do not intend to change. these are the basic principles, the basic reference values for the evolution of government deficits and government debt and the excessive deficit procedure as defined in the current article 104 of the treaty. it is not a question of discussing what is not subject to discussion because it is subject to discussion in the present treaty and will be in the future constitution. the aim is to discuss proposals to improve, strengthen, clarify the implementation and improve the degree of compliance with the framework provided for in the current treaty and developed, among others, in the so-called stability and growth pact. this framework is based on national economic policies but coordinated in budgetary policies which must respect the budget deficit limit of 3% and the debt criterion of 60% of gross domestic product. on this basis, the commission's ideas in the communication cover both economic policy coordination and budgetary coordination or the monitoring of budgetary policies. as regards economic policy, we believe that there is an obvious need to coordinate our actions in the field of structural reforms better and to strengthen our efforts to implement the lisbon agenda. europe needs to increase its growth potential and create more jobs and we cannot rely exclusively on one instrument - the stability and growth pact - to coordinate our economic policies. we must therefore make more effective use of the broad economic policy guidelines, an instrument which is by its nature more flexible than the stability and growth pact, and at the same time we must improve the implementation of the stability and growth pact by applying more and better the preventive measures or aspects of the pact by reinforcing peer pressure, and particularly during the favourable economic cycle. as regards budgetary coordination, the commission's proposals to strengthen and adapt the stability and growth pact are based on four main issues. first, the need to place greater emphasis on the level of indebtedness and the sustainability of public finances throughout the process of monitoring and surveillance of the development of public finances in each of the member states. in principle, compliance with the 3% ceiling for the maximum deficit should ensure an appropriate reduction in the level of indebtedness and the sustainability of public finances in each country. in practice, however, in many countries the debt situation has not developed as expected because of the application of exceptional measures or the emergence of implicit debts. we must therefore pay more attention to the evolution of debt as a complement to a close monitoring of the evolution of the public deficit. it should be clear that the sustainability problem does not only affect countries which already have high levels of debt, above the 60% reference value, but also other member states where the percentage of their debt to gdp is increasing or which, without increasing at the moment, already know that they have to face very important and very difficult challenges in the future. among others, those arising from demographic trends and the ageing of the population. secondly, the commission is aware of the need to take greater account of the different national situations when monitoring the budgetary developments in each country and, in particular, when determining the medium-term objective. in a union of 25 countries, it is not a question of creating a pact to the letter - as some have said - and the commission does not intend to do so - but of applying the economic logic which does not advise establishing a uniform medium-term objective for the development of public finances in each and every one of the countries of the enlarged union. at the same time, country-specific medium-term objectives should ensure that the 3% of gdp rule for government deficits is in any case met. this therefore ensures equal treatment for different member states, irrespective of their different sustainability situation of their public accounts. thirdly, the debate should address, in the commission's view, the need to implement measures quickly, to strengthen the use of the preventive measures of the stability and growth pact. we all know that in the late 1990s and early 2000s not all member states took advantage of the good economic situation in their economies, the good state of the business cycle, to consolidate their public finances sufficiently. as a result, in times of economic difficulties, it is not possible, or very difficult, to comply with the 3% rule at such times. on all these points - these first three blocks of ideas - there was, as the president-in-office of the council, mr zalm, said, almost immediate favourable reception by the council. the corrective part of the pact has already been the subject of further debate and will be in the future. in order to be consistent with our preventive measures, we also need, in the corrective part of the pact, in the excessive deficit procedure, to take account of the circumstances of each country and the point in time at which the economy of each country is in the cycle. how can this be done? by two possible procedures. first, the current definition of exceptional circumstances in the stability and growth pact can be improved, allowing a country to be excluded from the excessive deficit procedure, even if it is above 3% of the deficit, if it has been in a prolonged situation of growth below its potential level. in order to distinguish between periods of low cyclical and structural activity and to avoid weakening the supervisory framework, the other two requirements contained in the current exceptional circumstances clause should in any case be strictly applied. the deficit must be temporary and the deviation from the 3% threshold must not be too great. a second consideration is the need or possibility of adjusting the deficit correction path, the rate at which a country above 3% should bring its government deficit below that reference value. the differences between the cyclical situations of the different countries in this situation justify this approach. in any case, the principle of a rapid correction of an excessive deficit is maintained in the commission's communication, but the influence on budgetary results - as mr zalm has said - of other economic factors outside the intensity of the effort being called for, which the country concerned is developing, must be considered. in any event, there is an interrelation between these two elements included in the exceptional circumstances clause. there is, as they say in english, a trade-off. we cannot bet on the uncontrolled expansion of the margin of manoeuvre in both simultaneously. if more emphasis is placed on reviewing a country's entry into the excessive deficit procedure, the adjustment path will have to be more rigid. if the current rigidity in the opening of the excessive deficit procedure is maintained, the possibility of adjusting the timetables once the country has been brought into the excessive deficit procedure to restore a situation in accordance with the treaty may be considered. i am convinced that these improvements will underpin a strengthening of the economic governance framework for economic and monetary union, that these ideas and the debate we are going to undertake from this weekend onwards will not only not weaken the pact but strengthen it, because the weakness of a pact, the weakness of a fiscal framework does not only come from the theoretical brilliance of the rules which we all respect a priori or in theory, but also from the ability to apply those rules and, as the recent judgment of the court of justice of the european communities says, the decisions are for the member states meeting in the council. the commission retains its right to propose, but it is the council and the member states which have to apply the rules which they themselves have adopted when they adopted the treaty and the subsequent regulations. the member states cannot be asked to adopt rules which they themselves do not believe in. and if there is a feeling based on experience that some of the rules need adaptation, it is better to adapt than not to respect them, to keep them unchanged and then to break them, which has been the unfortunate situation, at times, of the stability and growth pact. the citizens have placed in us in 1997 when we discussed the introduction of the euro, also in this house. the stability and growth pact is a requirement of equity and sustainability. it is therefore pact reflects the simple but economically fundamental insight that today's debts are always tomorrow's taxes, and are borne by future generations. the com munity's budgetary position is not in line with the budgetary position of the member states. the rules of the pact allow and permit the temporary accumulation of deficits during the recovery, as has already been said, but these new debts must then be offset during the next recovery. in this context, the european commission's communication rightly raises the question of long-term sustainability and calls for a better link between the broad lines of economic policy and the stability and growth pact. the commission's recommendations, however, are critical of the commission's emphasis on the economic cycle, which is the subject of the communication. in total, the european commission's communication contains five key proposals, of which i can only evaluate one below for reasons of time, namely improved budgetary coordination and enforcement. a closer link between the commission's recommendations on the broad economic policy guidelines and the stability and growth pact is welcome, and has enabled the european commission to reinvigorate systemic competition in the europe of 25 and to make an important contribution towards achieving the objectives agreed in lisbon. in this respect, the proposals put forward here again for more transparency and accountability in the budgetary policies of the member states are to be fully supported, and it must be in the particular interest of all participants in monetary union to support the credibility of the stability and growth pact through transparent data.

going through a period of political instability; this may also have an impact on some of the measures being taken at the moment. the negative vote in the knesset two days ago raises a political creating difficulties within israeli political society as well. we are therefore in a situation where new political realignments in israel are very likely to take place in the coming weeks, possibly even leading to the formation of a coalition government. but in any case, it is also very likely that the elections which were due to take place in 2006 will have to be brought forward to 2005 for the reasons i have just mentioned. in any case, we are interested in the peace process not going any slower than it is going. ladies and gentlemen, the roadmap spoke of a peace process in which there should be two states by the end of 2005. in 2005 we will have, at most, the withdrawal of israeli forces from gaza, we will have no more. and that is a huge failure on the part of everybody and very specifically on the part of israel and palestine and on the part of the quartet and the international community. i would also like to say to you, ladies and gentlemen, that the latest statements made by some political figures in israel are statements which the european union cannot accept. these are the statements of a really unconscionable brazenness, at least for us. what has been said about the meaning of disengagement - the exit from gaza - the meaning of a total and absolute rejection of the roadmap, which the israeli government has signed, seems to me to be something that we must denounce in the clearest possible way. we cannot accept that way of working in politics. such statements create a lack of trust, not only in us, but in the entire arab world, in the neighbouring countries, in the palestinians themselves and in a good part of israeli society, and we cannot continue in this way. to say one thing and then say the opposite in the newspapers is not honest in politics. and it's not just anyone who says this, it's a person of weight, a significant and important person, one of the people closest to the prime minister of israel. that said, the question we all ask ourselves is: what to do? what can we do from a european perspective? ladies and gentlemen, mr president, the european union has a clear direction, set out in the roadmap, which is also the result of the efforts of the europeans, the americans, the united nations and the russian federation. we are defending it from the beginning to the end and we will not agree with those who do not defend it from the beginning to the end. we do, and therefore, whatever we want or can contribute at the moment, we want to do within that framework which is the roadmap. what can we do to speed up this process in the short and medium term? in the short term, i think we should work on four lines so that at the next council of ministers in march, and certainly at the european council in march, we can ratify them and put them into effect. the first is safety. the european union is ready and has a plan and a concept to help the palestinian authority improve its police conditions so that it can play its role in a serious and rigorous way, in law and order and in the fight against terrorism. we're willing to do that. we have the plan to do it, we have the people to do it and we have the will to do it. secondly, there are the reforms. the european union will do all it can to help the palestinian authority to complete the reform process it has begun. the palestinian authority leaders can be convinced, they can be sure that if they want to move forward on the path of reform, they will always find us by their side. thirdly, there are the economic actions. commissioner patten will speak about this in more detail, but in any case you should know that we are prepared to continue helping to ensure that this peace process does not suffer from a lack of resources from the european union from an economic point of view. but it must also be made clear that european citizens, who pay taxes in europe, cannot be paying money all the time if the operations financed do not lead to the desired goal, which is peace. and i would like to say that if the disengagement process, or the process of leaving gaza, is aimed solely and exclusively at gaza, the citizens and leaders of israel can be sure that they will not be able to count on the money of the european union. the gaza process must be part of a longer process, a process that really leads to the two states, which is the fundamental objective of the roadmap. and finally, fourthly, i think we have to work seriously on the electoral process. we must help to establish an electoral process in the territories, and that the palestinians can lead it; that there is an electoral commission that is reliable and that has the confidence of the people, so that the electoral process can result in a leadership - the one that the citizens of palestine want - that can put that country on the path towards its golden dream, which is the dream of many of us, the dream of two states. i said that about the short term, mr president. can we continue with just an incremental, step-by-step approach, or is it time to do something else? or is it time to take a longer leap, to play a much riskier role, if possible, but one that leads much more quickly to the final solution? we believe that the step by step, the small step by small step, is surely coming to an end and that, within the roadmap, progress can be made and progress can be made more rapidly if there is political will. we have it and, once the elections in the united states of america are held, we will try to continue working with them, with our russian friends and with our friends in the united nations, to see if it is possible to accelerate the roadmap, so that this slowness which generates suffering and frustration - without anything positive for the palestinians, for the israelis, for the region, for the neighbours, for ourselves and our societies - is ended and begins with a much faster progress that will lead us to the dream of all of us, which is - as i said before - the two states. we have talked a lot about the two states, but we have never defined what we want the palestinian state to be, what borders it will have. all these issues remain open and have not been closed. i would like to say again that from the point of view of the european union, some of the elements which form part of the final debate on these parameters are clear to us. for us the borders of that palestinian state must be the 1967 borders. we have said it very clearly, we said it at the foreign ministers' meeting on monday, we have said it through the european council and we are solemnly repeating it in this house today. and, from those 1967 borders, the two sides can negotiate any territorial exchanges they deem necessary. but that must be the basis of the negotiations and from there we should move - and i hope we can do so before the end of the year - on how to move more directly and more rapidly towards defining the final parameters, which can make this dream of so many people a reality and a political process which contradicts some of the statements made in recent days by responsible and respectable people on behalf of israel. after speaking as we have done in the past few days with the leaders of jordan, egypt and saudi arabia, i want to say to them that they all have the same feeling that, without knowing exactly where we are going, nor what the borders of the new palestinian state are, nor when that leap forward is going to take place, the stability of their own countries is at a certain level of risk. jordan is, in principle, a country whose borders are still undefined, which does not yet know what its neighbour will be and which wants and has the right to know what the borders of its new neighbour, the palestinian state, will be. mr president, the situation - as i said - is sad, frustrating for those who have devoted many hours of their lives to trying to find a way to peace. it is important that it be resolved, because the whole middle east - not just the peace process, but the whole middle east - is in a deep crisis and that deep crisis is something we all want to get out of. but we have to start by coming out very likely through a faster, more effective peace process, with more involvement from the international community and the key players, which are israel and palestine. mr president, i have little more to say to you this afternoon, but i want to say with all my heart that we will continue to work from now until the next council of ministers to see if we can put in place a small plan which, within the roadmap, can speed up the process in the way i have expressed myself to you. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with the sadness, the frustration and the emotion that all these issues arouse in the speaker - and in all of you - i say again that we will continue to work day and night to achieve this goal.

high representative. madam president, i am going to talk about georgia, a very important subject, and i am sure that the majority of the people here are very concerned about the situation there. from the outset of political change in georgia, the european union has been fully engaged with the new government and the new political leaders who have been in georgia since the so-called ‘rose revolution’. i would like to tell you what we have done so far. firstly, we have appointed a special representative, mr heikki talvitie, who represents us in the region, and particularly in georgia. the role he has played has been greatly appreciated by everybody, by president saakashvili, by the minister for foreign affairs, by the government as a whole, and by the countries of the region. he has been able to act as a link between georgia and russia, which, as you can imagine, is a very important element in the situation today. secondly, and very importantly, we have included georgia and two other countries in the region, azerbaijan and armenia, in the neighbourhood policy. this has been the most important way in which we were able to help these countries move closer to the european union. we did it rapidly, and you can imagine the happiness this decision has created for the people and leaders of georgia. i would also like to say that the european union has already organised a donors conference for georgia. it was a success, right after the change in government. in july we launched the first esdp operation for the rule of law in georgia. it is working very well. it is an innovation, one of the many operations and actions the european union can carry out among the whole panoply of capabilities we have for helping countries in transition. the situation in georgia is not good from an economic point of view. gdp has decreased by almost 60%, which is of very serious concern. 60% of the population are probably below the poverty line and there are still around 300 000 displaced persons as a result of the wars in georgia. i cannot finish talking about georgia without talking about the conflicts and the problems facing the country. georgia has solved one problem through the autonomy of ajaria, but there are still two big problems which will not be solved so easily: the problem of south ossetia and the problem of abkhazia. the oecd has a role to play there. mr talvitie, representing us, will continue to work on that. but the solution of those problems will not be as simple and easy as the one i mentioned before, which was resolved quite smoothly through the autonomy process. this is going to be more difficult. it is going to require a good understanding of russia. we are ready to play that role if necessary, but we have the impression that these two issues are going to take more time and will be more difficult. but in any case they have to be resolved. without the resolution of the problem there, georgia's integrity will never be a reality. i would also like to say a word on regional cooperation. georgia cannot be isolated from its two other neighbours in the southern caucasus: azerbaijan and armenia. we have a relationship with the three countries. we would like to construct a relationship with the three countries which is vivid, which is important and which is close to the european union and the european union dream. i therefore want to say that president saakashvili has the support of the european union. it was clear from the very beginning that he had enormous problems in front of him. we are going to help him with the reforms he has to make internally and in georgia's relations with neighbouring countries, in particular its relations with russia, which will be highly important. as you know, there are still russian troops in georgia. president saakashvili has said he will not accept forces from any other country in his territory and therefore he will give guarantees to the russians that they can leave without the risk of any forces from any other country appearing in georgia. georgia has a difficult time ahead and needs the help of its friends. here we are. we are friends of georgia.
commission. mr president, let me briefly address three questions. how far has georgia come since the 'rose revolution' eleven months ago? how have we tried to assist georgia in this process? what are the challenges ahead in eu–georgia relations? first of all, georgia's achievements. most importantly of course, all observers judged georgia's presidential and parliamentary elections in january and march of this year to be the freest and fairest in georgia's post-soviet history. georgia now has a president and government with a very strong popular mandate to carry out the profound political and economic reforms which we all know are so necessary. a good start has been made in addressing the structural problems facing georgia, tackling for example endemic corruption, which has harmed every facet of life in georgia. georgia's state finances have been put on a more stable path to recovery. revenue collection has increased, allowing the georgian government to pay salaries on time. reform of the law enforcement agencies has begun and a new tax code has been presented to the parliament. it is only a start, but georgia has done well in the last eleven months. how have we helped since november last year? firstly, we have offered consistent political support to the new leadership and we have encouraged it along the path of reform. we have been in close touch with it and with the mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. the ecb's annual report 2003 has a new format. it is clearer, it is more comprehensible, it has more detail, it has greater transparency even on the critical points of the current policy. this will give the reader, the public, better access to the ecb's policy in this report. we think that the ecb has done a good job overall. there are criticisms of the ecb in the original report by my colleague mr lipietz which we do not share. first of all, the interest rate policy. we do not think it is right to criticise the interest rate policy as a whole. we know that interest rate policy is a balancing act, but on the whole the ecb has managed to keep things in balance in 2003: the economy is developing, the euro is stable and we have low real interest rates. the second point of criticism, which we do not share, is that we believe that the ecb's responsibilities are clearly and well regulated, namely, first and foremost, price stability and moderate inflation rates. if that happens, then important conditions for economic growth and employment are in place, of course not enough, but we should not put the ecb in charge of full employment or economic growth. this would be a total burden on the ecb. this is a matter for national governments! commission. mr president, we have all seen the latest news about the large-scale job cuts that were announced a few days ago by a major automobile manufacturer. the commission fully understands the worries and sympathises with the workers in rüsselsheim, bochum, trollhättan and elsewhere. we are following these developments very closely using the community competences that are available to us to facilitate better industrial conditions for the car industry in europe. the sector's difficulties stem partly from the general economic downturn over the past few years. the low gdp growth rate in the eu has had its repercussions on the car industry too. thus we have seen a decline in sales of motor vehicles and a decline in employment in the automotive industry. therefore, improving general consumer confidence and economic dynamism is also crucial for the demand and sales of cars. competitiveness, economic reform and new industrial policy are now high on the political agenda of the commission and will receive even more focus in the new commission. we shall also soon learn how mr kok proposes to revise the lisbon strategy to put more weight on higher growth and better job creation. in order to be able to better assess the competitiveness of the car industry the commission has launched a study that we will publish in a few weeks time in the context of our annual competitiveness report. the study shows that the automotive industry contributes 6% to our manufacturing employment and 7% to manufacturing output in the union, making it a major driver in the european economy. its added value and employment have, however, declined between 2000 and 2002. a similar development in employment took place in the us and japan. our analysis of europe's strengths reveals that, due to the large home market, the european motor vehicle industry is well positioned to exploit economies of scale. moreover, due to the sophisticated demand, eu manufacturers get advance feedback from their customers, which helps them improve product quality. furthermore there is a high innovation capacity and research and development spending amongst the european automotive industry is at least as high as, or higher than, that in the us and japan. in terms of weaknesses, eu productivity is still lower than that in the us and japan. furthermore there is slow growth in the european home market, which means that as other markets continue to grow the demand advantages from the large european market may diminish over time. compared to the current level of productivity in the union, the level of labour costs presents a serious challenge for the car industry in some member states. labour costs per hour in the european union are still somewhat below those in the united states but significantly higher than those in japan and especially korea. we can best compete if we can offer better quality, better technology and better services that come with a car. this underlines the importance of innovation. as has been shown by some manufacturers, an agreement can also be reached with the workforce, aimed at reducing costs. for this to happen there has to be a common understanding between management and the workforce as to what objectives are to be achieved. such agreements make sense if they can be used to save employment, to keep manufacturing locations and to make the car industry more competitive. with regard to threats, our studies see a danger that major innovations are not stimulated by european regulations. future regulation must therefore take into account the long-term competitiveness of the car industry and the need for manufacturers to be able to sell their products and similar products in europe and on the whole world market. this must be addressed by policies of better regulation, which is a major challenge for both of us, the commission as well as for parliament. the commission is currently considering setting up a high-level group to analyse major challenges affecting the automobile sector and to identify ways and means to improve the industrial framework conditions in the sector. this high-level group should also focus on the cumulative impact of legislation on the sector's competitiveness. it is up to the new commission to take a position on the setting up of such a group. commissioner verheugen, or rather vice-president-designate verheugen, said at his hearing in front of you in the european parliament that he is considering setting up such a group. i will certainly support him if he chooses to do so. in conclusion, the commission is doing its utmost to offer the best possible industrial and innovative framework conditions for the car industry, for the european automotive industry. we need to further develop dialogue in the sector with the main stakeholders involved. moreover, we must revise the lisbon strategy of growth and employment to revitalise economic dynamism and to strengthen consumer demand on our continent. growth and employment must indeed be put centre stage in all union activities.

commission. my experience over the years, not only in the case of burma but also in other cases, has been that when the commission is asked to police a sanctions regime it does so as diligently as possible. the diligence with which we pursue these policies is not always as popular with some member states as it might be. sanctions can be sometimes a rather pavlovian foreign policy reaction: what is important is to examine the credibility of sanctions and to ensure that, where you put them in place, you apply them as rigorously as possible. i was unable to give the honourable member who asked the first question all the information he would have liked, but i have tried - as i am sure that my successors will try - to be as open on this as possible. it is perfectly legitimate for parliament to want to be absolutely clear about these matters: about what is being done in the name of human rights policy in burma and about how we are trying to make a success of an objective which we presumably all share both in principle and in practice. that is, to secure the release of an extraordinarily brave woman and those who, with her, have fought not just for democracy, better human rights and civil liberties in burma but also for a better deal for an extremely talented people who have been impoverished by totalitarianism.
question no 36 by mr von wogau (h-0352/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: review of the financial regulation and the external action procurement procedure will the commission, in the light of the forthcoming review of the financial regulation, submit a proposal to simplify the external action procurement procedures, in particular as regards military and non-military crisis management measures?
commission. first it should be stated that operations having military or defence implications cannot be financed from the community budget – i have spent too long looking at the provisions of article 28(3) – and are therefore financed on an intergovernmental basis. as regards the financing of non-military crisis management operations, the rules referred to in the question are laid down not only in the financial regulation, but also in its implementing rules. the implementing rules already offer simplified procurement procedures for crisis situations in external relations, such as the use of negotiated procedures. it should be recalled that such simplified procedures constitute derogations from the normal procedures. moreover, parliament monitors their use by the commission and a special report on their use is presented every year to the budgetary authority. arrangements for crisis management operations under the cfsp are currently being reviewed in the light of the functional needs of these operations, which it should be possible to accommodate within the existing framework of rules. for the longer term, the financial regulation provides for a review every three years, or whenever necessary. the commission undertook to report on its experiences after the first two years of application of these new rules, that is, by the spring of 2005. this review will cover both the financial regulation and its implementing rules in order to see if, in the light of experience, any modifications to the rules are necessary, including the procurement rules for external actions in general and for crisis management operations in particular. i hope that is relatively clear.

commission. i have some sympathy with what the honourable member says in relation to both bosnia and macedonia. at present, each time there is a crisis-management operation, all the necessary supplies and equipment have to be procured from scratch. however, the contracting, which obviously takes some time, cannot begin until the head of mission has been appointed and has engaged his own staff. therefore we have to find some way to allow the procurement to begin before the crisis-management operation is formally adopted so that the supplies are available as soon as the operation starts, or very shortly thereafter. we could obviously provide technical assistance with this preparatory work, but i am sure this is one of the factors that will be taken into account in the review of the implementing rules which i mentioned earlier. in my experience it is not always possible for us to operate as rapidly as we would like, and that is because of the rules which have been put in place, usually with good reasons - greater transparency, proper budgetary procedure, etc. unfortunately, when people draw up those rules they do not always think about the real world in which we have to operate.

question no 40 by mr czarnecki (h-0369/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: turkey's accession to the european unionthe author of the question takes note of the european commission's strategic decision to open formal negotiations with turkey on its accession to the european union. in view of the contradictory reports on this subject, can the commission say what impact the possible accession of turkey in 2014 or 2015 will have on the financial resources for the 10 new member states of the european union, in particular in the area of the common agricultural policy and regional policy?
the commission. first of all, thank you for the compliment. as in the case of poland, the question of balancing regional disparities will of course play a major role in the case of turkey, should it join. but it is really not possible to say at this stage how this will be financed. i would just like to point out that there is a ceiling of 4% of gdp for the transfer of resources to new member states and also to old member states. that means there's not an infinite amount that can be easily forwarded. but for large member states such as spain, italy and poland, this 4% threshold has never been reached and will never be reached. it is therefore reasonably safe to assume that the case of turkey, when it comes to that, cannot be compared with estonia or lithuania, but that turkey must be compared with spain or poland. then we're going to be on a whole different scale.
question no 41 by mr bernd posselt (h-0300/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: administration and justice in romania and bulgariawhat measures is the commission taking to improve the functioning of the administration and the judiciary in romania and bulgaria?
the commission. - mr president, this is a very complex subject. the commission attaches great importance to the ongoing reforms of the public administration and the judiciary in both countries. these reforms must ensure that both countries are not only able to meet the membership requirements, but above all that they are able to effectively fulfil their obligations as member states after accession. romania has made recent concrete progress, for example with the formal adoption of a strategy to accelerate public administration reform and a 2003 strategy on judicial reform, and the adoption of three basic laws on judicial reform in june 2004. however, romania has yet to ensure the successful implementation of these measures. in bulgaria, after much pressure, i myself adopted a strategy for the reform of public administration over a year ago, and its implementation is also progressing well overall in bulgaria. however, i must make it clear that considerable efforts are still needed to improve the organisation of work, the administrative capacity required to implement the acquis and, in particular, the management structures of the bulgarian administration. the commission has also adopted a communication on the implementation of the eu's new strategy for the prevention of corruption and organised crime. the commission will closely monitor further developments in this area. the commission has supported these reforms with pre-accession assistance and in close cooperation with other donors, including the member states. public administration reform and judicial reform are among the top priorities to be promoted under the phare multiannual programming for 2004-06. in addition, informal committees on public administration reform and judicial reform have been established to conduct a structured dialogue with both countries on these issues and to monitor and support the development of operational capacity in both areas.

question no 43 by mr papastamkos (h-0333/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: community action for border regions - greece the community action to combat the effects of enlargement in regions of eu member states sharing a common border with the candidate countries also included five greek regions. the commission itself has taken the view that (western, central and eastern) macedonia and thrace are by far the most disadvantaged in terms of income, labour market dynamics, infrastructure and human resources. can the commission therefore state what its assessment so far is of the use of community funds for these regions? what will be the direction of community action after 2006 in view of the prospective accession of bulgaria and romania and the start of accession negotiations between the eu and turkey, especially in view of the fact that greece borders all three candidate countries? what measures have been taken with regard to crossborder infrastructures aimed at integrating the territories?
commission. - thank you very much, mr president, for your kind acknowledgement. let me try to explain this in my own words. greece has three different programmes in its north. we have the programmes relating to crossborder cooperation with bulgaria, a future member state. as soon as bulgaria becomes a member, this programme will expire and instead there will be a normal interreg programme on the border between bulgaria and greece, as is the practice between member states. but that doesn't mean it's less money. it's just a different program. greece has a joint programme with the neighbouring countries of albania and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, which are not yet candidate countries. that is why we have a different programme. the commission plans to combine these instruments into a single neighbourhood programme for simplification. this will be the case throughout the next financial year. i do not feel that we are going to have less resources at this frontier, quite the contrary, considering the high priority given to the western balkan countries in our strategic considerations. thirdly, we have the border with the candidate country turkey, where, as a result of the intensive cooperation which is now being established with turkey, resources are being made available in an increased scale in this border region as well. in general, it can be said that the situation in the greek border regions will change in some cases purely technically, but that it is not necessary to expect that there will be a loss of resources, rather the opposite.
question no 44 will be answered in writing. question no 45 by mr sjöstedt (h-0313/04) subject: the commission's proposal to the council on the future of the european union subject: future of the alcohol monopoly companyin spring 2004, advocate general phillipe leger of the european court of justice argued that the state pharmacy monopoly was contrary to the community competition principles. the judgment in the so-called hanner case is expected later this year, but in general the european court of justice follows the opinion of the advocate general. in view of this attitude towards pharmacies, how does the commission assess the future of the swedish alcohol monopoly?
the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, although the court of justice may adopt the opinion of the advocate general, it must be stressed that this opinion is not legally binding, either on the commission or on any other party. the same applies to the opinion delivered on 25 may 2004 by advocate general léger in case c-438/02 åklagaren v krister hanner, concerning the compatibility of apoteket, the monopoly for the distribution of medicinal products in sweden, with certain provisions of the treaties relating to the free movement of goods and the right of establishment (articles 28, 31 and 43). as regards systembolaget, the distribution system for alcoholic beverages in sweden, the court of justice has already ruled on the compatibility of that monopoly with article 31 of the treaty in its judgment of 23 october 1997 in franzén. the structure and operation of state monopolies must be organised in such a way as to exclude any discrimination between nationals of member states as regards the conditions of supply and disposal, so that trade in goods from another member state is not disadvantaged de jure or de facto in comparison with a national product. after a thorough examination of the systembolaget system as regards the points of sale, the choice of products and the promotional activities, the court decided that the monopoly sales structure of systembolaget was compatible with article 31 of the treaty. as things stand, the franzén judgment provides the commission with legal guidance in assessing the compatibility of systembolaget with eu rules.
commission. i have nothing to add at this stage.

commission. unfortunately europe, like every other area of the world, is no stranger to national disasters. there have been a number in recent years. i am sure that some of us will remember the huge floods in germany and austria only a few years ago. with the support of parliament, the commission has tried to put in place appropriate mechanisms, within the limits of the financial resources available. these included the monitoring of state aid - subsidies or contributions from national budgets - and also direct contributions from the community budget. as regards the 'tremonti bis' law referred to in mrs sbarbati's oral question, the commission was not questioning whether companies suffering the consequences of natural disasters should be helped. the issue was whether the way the law was formulated enabled that objective to be met.
question no 48 by mr staes (h-0331/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: inquiry into the market for ink cartridgesin its reply to written question e-0699/03 oj c 33 e, 6.2.2004, p. 71. the commission states that it has recently initiated proceedings concerning, inter alia, ink cartridges and printers. it is currently examining the behaviour of several undertakings on the markets concerned in the light of the community competition rules. can the commission state what progress it has made in this matter and whether the cartridge and printer market has passed the examination for compatibility with the community competition rules? if not, can it provide any reasons for the termination of the investigation?
commission. thank you for that observation. i can assure you that the commission will make public all the relevant elements. we are not yet in a position to find out whether there has been an infringement. you will certainly be aware that the commission does not have the role of a price regulator. we live and work in a social market economy and it is of paramount importance that the commission ensures that the conditions for competition are in place, pursuant to european law. these may or may not lead to consumers perceiving prices to be high. it would not be right in an efficient market economy for the commission to set prices. this is not an option. but i am sure that just as this commission did, the incoming commission will closely monitor all the phenomena which might violate competition rules, causing adverse effects for european consumers.

i'm sorry to interrupt you, sir. from what i've heard so far, that doesn't apply to the question, and you can only ask specifically about the subject here. question no 52 by catherine stihler (h-0288/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: reaction to recent studies on foetal alcohol syndrome (fas) the extent of fetal alcohol syndrome (fas) and the best recommendation for expectant mothers remain controversial. a recent study by dr. raja mukherjee, london, has found that the intake of any amount of alcohol can be harmful and that one in every 100 newborns is harmed by their mother's drinking during pregnancy, but the dark figure is very high. studies in the united states, south africa, and scandinavia show that 1 in 300 infants is affected by fas. affected children may have problems with memory, concentration, hyperactivity, physical abnormalities, and a decreased iq. further research on fas is necessary. however, high levels of alcohol consumption are known to be harmful to the unborn child, and some eu governments recommend a limit of 1 to 2 units of alcohol per week for pregnant women. does the commission therefore intend to introduce eu legislation requiring that alcoholic beverages be labelled with a warning about the potential harm to unborn children?
commission. thank you for that supplementary question and for your kind words, mrs stihler. i appreciate that. as you may know, dg sanco is at present preparing a community strategy to reduce alcohol-related harm, as called for in the council conclusions in 2001. several areas for action have been identified as key areas. one of them is consumer information, to improve awareness of the risks connected with the consumption of alcoholic beverages. at the moment the draft proposals concern the legal and practical feasibility of having health warnings on the containers of alcoholic beverages, as well as at points of sale. these would include information on, for instance, pregnancy. if the public health authorities do not move in and occupy the field, it might well be occupied by industry. that is not entirely satisfactory, because the information being made available by the industry might not be consistent with best public health practice. i look forward to further discussion of this important issue in the future.
question no 53 by mr papadimoulis (h-0298/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: situation of slaughterhouses in greecethe commission's food and veterinary office carries out regular inspections in the member states to check, among other things, whether the community rules on hygiene in slaughterhouses are being complied with. following the recent inspection visits to greece, can the commission state to what extent greek slaughterhouses and meat markets, such as the rendi meat market in athens, are in line with european standards? does the commission consider that the modernisation measures are satisfactory or that there are still shortcomings in the control of food safety in greece? what measures has it taken or will it take to ensure that greece complies with its obligations under the relevant community legislation?
commission. two inspections carried out by the commission's food and veterinary office in greece, in july 2003, march and april 2004, revealed breaches of community requirements with regard to procedures for licensing abattoirs and respect of hygiene requirements. these findings confirm the results of earlier fvo missions. based on commission recommendations, commitments were received from the greek authorities on action to rectify these deficiencies. as regards the new rentis market, there has been slipping in the timetable notified by the greek authorities for its construction. according to our latest information, the construction works are scheduled for completion in mid­2006. despite the fact that the commission has had a number of high­level contacts with the greek authorities in recent years about the food control system, progress has not been satisfactory. this relates to the specific issue of insufficient staffing levels in the greek veterinary service to ensure effective implementation of eu veterinary legislation. that is why, in may 2004, the commission sent a letter of formal notice to the greek authorities urging them to remedy this situation. in the absence of appropriate assurances from the greek authorities, the commission sent a reasoned opinion to greece on 18 october, asking the greek government to address effectively the problem of understaffing in its veterinary services within a period of two months. failure to do so could lead the commission to bring the case before the court of justice. the commission is also considering similar action in relation to the control systems in greece for the approval of red meat establishments. the commission has been keeping the situation in greece under close review and intends to continue to ensure that the necessary corrective actions are taken.

productivity, growth and employment. there are two reasons for this: the first is due to factors over which we have little control, such as external indicators, world economic influences, oil prices, implementation plans and to make the lisbon project the focus of their national policies. otherwise it won't work. i agree with mr watson that whether we are as good as the americans in 2010 is an foundation of european policy. but if we want to have the highest possible environmental and social standards, then we also need the most competitive economy possible. we need competitive industries and competitive companies. the question of competitiveness is not about making the greatest possible profits for individuals, but about making our economies strong enough to meet the great social goals of high environmental and social standards. the truth is that in europe we use formulas which conceal completely different ideas. i noticed that in this debate. for example, there were very different ideas about the european social model: it has been argued that we have too high a level of protection for workers in europe. it has been argued here that we have too few social rights. it has been argued here that we need reforms in the sense of a reduction in social rights; it has been argued here that we need reforms in the sense of more social rights. there is no consensus in europe on what this term 'social model' actually means. if i have the opportunity in the next few years to be involved in this policy area, i will not be part of this policy of concealment and silence. i will make it clear that there are conflicts here, that these conflicts must be named, that the decisions must be made in full awareness of the fact where the conflicts actually lie, and that these council. mr president, the european security and defence policy is on the brink of a historic step. the eu's first military crisis management operation, operation althea, will start on 2 december. in the development of the esdp, we have made great progress from concepts and capabilities to concrete actions. like the first eu police mission, the first military operation will take place in bosnia and herzegovina. the preparations for the deployment of operation althea after sfor leaves bosnia and herzegovina are well advanced. an operational concept has been approved, force generation has taken place, and 11 third countries have been invited to contribute to the operation. a committee of contributors has had its first meeting and the operations plan has been approved by the council. operation althea will be an eu-led operation, with the use of nato assets and capabilities. therefore, the deputy saceur was appointed operation commander in early july. the operation's hq has been established in mons. in early october the force headquarters in sarajevo reached initial operational capability with a view to reaching full operational capability by early december, when authority is transferred from sfor. people might consider the transfer of the operation from sfor to the eu a big and risky step. they might have doubts about the capabilities of the eu mission. however they are wrong, if only because 80% of the sfor forces have transferred to althea, while the departing 20%, which are us forces, will be replaced by additional european forces. all the eu member states currently contributing to sfor will continue their contributions in althea. however, althea is not just an eu operation. third countries like morocco, bulgaria, romania, norway and turkey will participate as well. i am very pleased about their participation, because it shows that it is not just the eu that cares about bosnia and herzegovina. as members of the committee of contributors, these countries will have the same rights and obligations as the eu member states taking part in the operation in terms of its day-to-day management. no effort has been spared in ensuring a smooth transition from nato to the eu and that includes the delineation of tasks between althea and the remaining nato headquarters in sarajevo, arrangements on the availability and use of reserve forces and on the sharing of intelligence. the eurfor commanding officer and the commander of the remaining nato headquarters will be based at the same camp, ensuring operational coordination. nato itself also remains present in bosnia and herzegovina. we therefore have a nato strategic reserve for support in emergencies. this can be used for both nato and operation althea. this is a good example of the pragmatic and efficient use of limited resources. it also emphasises the good cooperation between the eu and nato. with the transition from nato to the eu, the last phase of military presence will start. the accent will no longer be on the prevention of inter-ethnic fighting but on assisting civil and military reforms. after that, a military presence can be withdrawn. with althea, we are contributing to the security and stability of bosnia and herzegovina, which is important to the reforms in that country. at the same time, operation althea is – dare i say – the final element in a comprehensive european union policy towards bosnia and herzegovina. it is also part of our broader strategy for the balkans. the combined activities in the political, economic development and security fields mutually reinforce each other. the situation in the country has a direct impact on the region and on the eu. we therefore have a clear interest in its stability and prosperous development. eu involvement is not only in its interests but also in our own and, given our comprehensive and coherent approach, it is only logical that the eu has taken over the nato operation. the ultimate objective is to put bosnia on track towards the eu and this will be achieved through the strength and stabilisation association process. the eu military mission, together with other eu activities such as the eu police mission, the eu monitoring mission and the cards development programme, will complement that process a comprehensive approach reflects our belief that the future of bosnia lies firmly in europe. it exemplifies our long-term commitment. it is now up to the bosnian people to make the vision come true. they will eventually have to decide whether to join the european political and economic union. such a choice requires fundamental reforms of state, economic and judicial structures. equally, they will have to confirm the decision to join the european community of values. such a decision requires an environment of tolerance, dialogue, respect for religious freedoms and a tough stance in words and deeds against the impunity of war criminals. the right political will and popular support by the bosnians, combined with our comprehensive role, could and should lead bosnia away from conflict into a stable and peaceful future, a future in which our special representative lord ashdown will play an ever more important role. let me conclude by saying that bosnia and herzegovina is on the right track. stability and security are increasing and, with its integration into euro-atlantic structures, the country is moving more and more from the area of dayton to the area of brussels. however, much remains to be done, because we are still concerned about the lack of cooperation with icty, particularly in the case of the republika srpska. icty cooperation is an important criterion for closer relations with the eu and nato. here bosnia and herzegovina will have to deliver. i hope the reforms of the defence and police apparatus, one of the key tasks of althea, will also bear fruit in that field. in that way operation althea will bring even more benefit to the people of bosnia and herzegovina in their quest for a durable and just peace.
commission. i am extremely glad to have this opportunity to say a few words about bosnia and herzegovina, just two weeks before the handover to eufor on 2 december. the launching of the althea mission is an important event: important because it will be the first significant military operation undertaken under the european security and defence policy. the transfer from nato has required long and detailed discussions because it was crucial to get things right from the very start. my colleagues mr solana and mr de hoop scheffer deserve a great deal of credit for securing a successful outcome. i know some will be concerned that a brand new military mission in bosnia sends a signal that the country continues to suffer from significant instability. that would, in my judgement, be an entirely wrong conclusion to draw. last spring the north atlantic council ministerial meeting noted an 'improved security environment in bosnia and herzegovina'. as a result they decided to reduce the number of troops committed to sfor from 12 000 to 7 000. i have been visiting bosnia for several years and i can personally attest to the transformation which has come over the country during that period. it would be the height of folly to take for granted the undoubted improvements which have occurred. all that is happening is that europe is taking on more direct responsibility for its own continent – not before time, some might say. however, there will be a review of the operation every six months. this will take account of its duration, as well as its size and configuration. there is no question of keeping troops in bosnia unnecessarily; as soon as conditions permit, the number of troops can be reduced and eventually the mission will come to an end. it is important at this time to recognise that bosnia’s european future will assume growing importance as the military presence continues to reduce in size. bosnia, like all the countries of the western balkans, has a clear european perspective as a potential candidate country. last november the commission published a feasibility study setting out 16 points on which the country needed to make significant progress before a recommendation could be made to the european council to start negotiations on a stabilisation and association agreement. although there has been progress since then, i am disappointed to end my mandate as commissioner without being able to give bosnia the green light. i very much hope that my successor, commissioner rehn, will be able to do so early in his new mandate. once he did so, the council would have to accept his assessment and a negotiating mandate would then have to be agreed. only then could negotiations start. there is no reason why they could not do so some time during 2005. if bosnia is to make progress on this timescale, a number of things are required. first, the authorities have to make further progress on the legislation associated with the 16 points. much has been done here, but there are continuing blockages in areas like vat and public broadcasting. second, bosnia has to recognise that passing laws has little utility if they are not implemented properly. there is still a great deal of work to be done here. third, the commission indicated in the feasibility study that it would expect proper cooperation with the high representative in his reform agenda, as provided for in the dayton paris peace accords. one crucial area here is the question of police reform. i very much hope that, by the end of the year, mr wilfried martens will be able to report agreement on the way forward. finally, there is the question of the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia. bosnia herzegovina is a member of the united nations and a signatory to dayton. as i have made clear on a number of occasions, there can be no dilution of the absolute requirement for full cooperation with the tribunal. this is fundamental to bosnia’s prospects for further movement through the stabilisation and association process. it is a crucial test of bosnia’s commitment to its international obligations and to the rule of law. it is also a fundamental part of the process of allowing the victims of the atrocities to let go of the past. allowing those accused of terrible human rights abuses to remain free makes it impossible for the communities to be properly reconciled. next week the chief prosecutor, mrs carla del ponte, will be reporting to the united nations security council on the cooperation of the countries of the western balkans with the tribunal. up until now, she has been quite clear that republika srpska has not been cooperating at all. it is indeed a disgraceful matter that not one indictee has been transferred by the republika srpska to the hague, although there are reports today that some war crime suspects have been arrested by republika srpska for trial locally. this is welcome news, but republika srpska will be judged by the international community on its cooperation with the tribunal on cases which fall under its jurisdiction. it is on that issue that mrs del ponte will be reporting to the security council. i have no reason to expect that her report will be positive on republika srpska. if that is indeed the case, lord ashdown will have to consider his response. certainly, it is intolerable that the prospects for the whole country to make progress towards joining the european union and nato are being compromised in this way. i urge the political leadership of republika srpska to take action now to fulfil their obligations. if they do not, they will be responsible for any consequences which flow from their failure. honourable members, the people of bosnia herzegovina suffered the most from the balkan wars in the 1990s. now they have emerged from that terrible period and have a clear chance of creating a real country with a genuine prospect of joining our european family. as i leave the commission, i wish them every success and i look forward to hearing of their progress in the months to come. which, under the treaty, the president of the commission is guarantor. with regard to the replacement of commissioners, we must make a distinction between the current situation, which foresees no role for either the commission president or parliament, and the future situation under the constitution. the constitution will bring the procedure for replacing commissioners closer to the procedure for the confirmation of the commission at the start of its mandate. in this transitional phase, i can therefore agree that new commission members should not appear officially before this parliament until they have met with the relevant parliamentary committee. as regards their appearance before council, that is not entirely in my hands, since a nominated new commissioner will have to carry out duties linked to his or her portfolio. in the event of a reshuffle of my team, i accept a similar obligation that commissioners whose portfolios change should not appear officially before this parliament until they have met with the relevant parliamentary committee. with regard to points 2 and 5 (d), your resolution suggests that we have not yet taken the necessary steps to avoid potential conflicts of interest. yesterday i explained the detailed arrangements for dealing with potential conflict of interest problems that might arise in a portfolio. let us now implement them. we will have the opportunity to assess their effectiveness at a later stage. i will make any further changes that prove necessary in the light of experience. with regard to point 5 (e), as i indicated in july, i share parliament's view of the need to strengthen multiannual programming and strategic planning, together with the council. i will therefore present to you in january draft proposals for the five-year strategic objectives of the union, which should be jointly adopted by all institutions. i will listen to your debate on the subject in december and take account of your main concerns. this anticipates this important new area of cooperation, also provided for in the constitution. now points 5 (f) and 5 (g). our relationship must be built on trust and regular contacts. my team will therefore give priority to appearing before this parliament. both i and vice-president wallström intend to maintain regular and active contact with the conference of presidents. the announcement of commission decisions and proposals to parliament reflects the current arrangements under the framework agreement, which i am, of course, willing to respect. nevertheless, i believe that this has not always been been implemented satisfactorily, either for the parliament or for the commission, particularly as regards communicating effectively to the wider public what the union does. i hope that we can discuss improvements to this arrangement, focused on identifying the most important proposals deserving the attention of parliament and our joint communication effort. presentation of these proposals should be timed as far as possible to coincide with plenary sessions. if we can do this, i would argue for greater flexibility on other more routine initiatives. point 5 (h). the commission already explains how it will follow up the positions of parliament on legislative proposals. experience shows that this mechanism is useful and i will be happy to extend it to positions taken by parliament in cases other than legislation. point 5 (i). we need to distinguish between issues related to the flow of information between the commission and the european parliament and issues linked more generally to weightiest and most significant dossiers currently facing the union. the council is therefore grateful to have been given the chance of setting out briefly how it is envisaged that this dossier should be dealt with. as you will be aware, the timetable for finalising work was laid out in the multiannual strategic programme for 2004-2006, adopted by the european council in december 2003. thus, with the majority of the commission’s financial and legislative proposals already on the table, work is currently under way within the council, aimed at possibly reaching decisions on principles and guidelines this month. the intention is to achieve political agreement before the june 2005 european council so that both the framework itself and the detailed legislation can finally be adopted by the end of 2005. preparatory work on new community programmes would thereafter be carried out throughout 2006 so that they could be implemented from the beginning of the new financial perspective
